title: Your AI office in 3D
does: Sets up your team's office in 3D on your own laptop: one desk per AI employee, today's board, and whatever accessories you ask for. Say "add a cat" and watch it appear.
prompt:
I want my AI team's office in 3D, running on my own laptop, built on the JTL HQ base (github.com/jtlgrowth/hq-base).

Ask me three things first, all at once, with options:
1. My company name and what we sell, in one line.
2. Who is on my team. If this folder has a roster.json from the /hire skill, read it (and docs/team/) and show me who you found. If not, ask me for up to six names and a one-line job each.
3. Which accessories to start with. Offer these and let me pick several: a coffee corner, a lounge set, plants by the desks, a bookshelf, a TV wall, a reading nook, an office cat, my logo on the wall.

Then do this yourself, do not just tell me how:
1. Get the base into a folder called "hq" here: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/jtlgrowth/hq-base hq. Then read hq/CLAUDE.md and follow its rules. Never edit the base files.
2. Write my company into hq/company.json. Write my team into hq/team.json, one desk each, or leave it as [] if you are reading roster.json.
3. If there is a brief-*.md or today's daily note in this folder, put its top three to-dos on the board in hq/tasks.md as "- [ ]" lines. If not, ask me for three things I am doing today.
4. Add the accessories I picked to hq/accessories.json, using only the ids in hq/ACCESSORIES.md. Place them with "near" (a teammate's name) or "spot" (lounge, pantry, entrance, back-left and so on).
5. Start it in the background: node hq/server.mjs. Open the address it prints (usually http://127.0.0.1:4747) in my browser.

When you are done, tell me the address, how to start it again tomorrow, and remember this rule: when I say "add a ___ to the office", you edit hq/accessories.json and I watch it appear.

To check it worked: the page opens, every teammate sits at a desk with their name over it, and the accessories I picked are in the room.
run_note: Base verified 2026-09-19: github.com/jtlgrowth/hq-base, 20/20 tests on a fresh clone, CI on ubuntu, macos and windows; a live accessories.json edit appeared in the open page in 2.3 s. Outcome video recorded 2026-09-19 on the base with a sample team (Sunrise Café), accessories added by writing accessories.json during the take. A full Claude Code run of this prompt waits on the demo login.

title: Obsidian second brain setup
does: Creates an Obsidian vault folder with a daily note template, a clients folder, an inbox note, and wires your CLAUDE.md to read it.
prompt:
I want a second brain in Obsidian (a free notes app, obsidian.md) that you can read and write to.

Ask me two things first:
1. Where should the vault folder live on my computer.
2. What do I call the folder (a name like a business name or "notes" is fine).

Then do this yourself, do not just tell me how:
1. Create the folder, and inside it: a "Daily" folder, a "Clients" folder, and an "Inbox.md" file for anything I drop in without sorting it.
2. Create "Daily/template.md" with a simple daily note shape: date, three priorities, notes, open loops.
3. Create today's daily note from that template.
4. Add a short section to my CLAUDE.md (or create one if I do not have one) that tells you this vault exists, where it lives, and that you should read the Inbox and today's daily note when I ask what is going on.

When you are done, tell me the exact folder path, list the files you created, and tell me how to open the vault in the Obsidian app (I install Obsidian myself, you do not need to).

To check it worked: open the vault folder in Finder or Obsidian and confirm Daily, Clients, Inbox.md and today's dated note are all there.

title: Morning brief from inbox and calendar
does: Reads today's calendar export or a pasted inbox dump and writes a 10-line brief with the three things to do first.
prompt:
I want a morning brief.

Ask me one thing first: do I want to paste in today's calendar (copy it from Google Calendar or your phone) and a rough dump of what is in my email inbox right now, or do I have a calendar export file (.ics or .csv) to point you to.

Once I give you that, read it and write a file called "brief-[today's date].md" with exactly this shape:
1. A one-line summary of how full today is (light, normal, packed).
2. The three things to do first, in order, and why those three over everything else.
3. Every meeting today with the time and who it is with.
4. Anything in the inbox dump that looks urgent or time-sensitive, each in one line.
5. One thing I could cancel or move if today gets tight.

Keep the whole file to about 10 lines of actual content, no filler.

When it is done, print the brief in the chat as well as saving the file, and tell me the file path.

To check it worked: read the brief back and see if the three things to do first actually match what matters most to you today. If they do not, tell Claude what it got wrong so it can fix the rule for next time.
run_note: Ran clean (exit 0) on a pasted calendar and inbox dump. Wrote brief-2026-09-15.md: load level, three do-first items in order with reasons, all three meetings, three flagged inbox items, one item to cut if tight. Read back correctly, matched the sample data. Video recorded 2026-09-16.

title: Reply drafter in your voice
does: Learns from three past replies you paste, then drafts three replies to a new message.
prompt:
I want you to learn how I write and draft replies for me.

Ask me for two things first:
1. Three examples of real replies I have sent before (emails, chats, anything), pasted in full so you can see my actual voice.
2. The new message I need to reply to right now.

From the three examples, work out: how formal or casual I am, how long my replies usually run, whether I use exclamation points or emoji, and how I usually open and close a message. Do not ask me to describe my own voice, read it from the examples.

Then write a file called "voice-notes.md" with what you learned in plain bullet points, so you do not have to re-learn it next time I ask.

Then draft three replies to the new message: one safe and short, one warmer and longer, one that says no or pushes back if that fits the situation. Label each one clearly.

When you are done, tell me which of the three you would send and why.

To check it worked: read the three drafts out loud. If none of them sound like something you would actually type, tell Claude what is off (too stiff, too long, wrong greeting) and have it redo voice-notes.md before drafting again.
run_note: Ran clean (exit 0) on three sample past replies plus one new message. Wrote voice-notes.md (formal level, po usage, length, sign-off pattern) then printed three labeled drafts in chat (safe, warmer, pushback) and picked one with a stated reason. Matches the prompt's shape; drafts were not asked to save to a file so none were, which is correct per the prompt text. Video recorded 2026-09-16.

title: Weekly numbers one-pager
does: From a pasted or CSV set of sales rows, writes a one-page HTML with this week vs last week.
prompt:
I want a one-page report comparing this week's sales to last week's.

Ask me one thing first: do I have a CSV file of sales rows to point you to, or should I paste the rows in directly (date, amount, and whatever else I have, like item or customer).

Once you have the rows, split them into this week and last week by date, then write a single self-contained file called "weekly-numbers.html" that shows, in plain readable HTML with basic styling (no build tools, it must open by double-clicking):
1. Total sales this week vs last week, and the percent change.
2. Number of sales (transactions) this week vs last week.
3. The best day this week and the worst day this week.
4. Top 3 items or customers this week if that data is in the rows.

Use plain numbers, peso sign if the amounts look like pesos, and one simple color to mark up or down. No jargon, no unexplained charts.

When it is done, tell me the file path and open it if you can, or tell me to double-click it.

To check it worked: open weekly-numbers.html in your browser and confirm the this-week and last-week totals actually match what you expected from your own memory of the week.
run_note: Ran clean (exit 0) on 14 pasted CSV-style rows split across two weeks. Wrote weekly-numbers.html, self-contained, opens without a build step; confirmed it starts with a valid DOCTYPE and inline styling and a totals card. Video recorded 2026-09-16.

title: Hire your next seat
does: Walks the public hire skill to add one more AI employee, picking the role from what the business does.
prompt:
I already have one AI employee hired with the hire skill. I want to hire my next one.

Use the hire skill (it is already installed) to walk me through this. Before you start the skill's own questions, ask me: what is the one task in my business that eats the most time right now, the one I would hand off first if I could.

From my answer, recommend the type of employee that fits best (someone who finds things, sorts things, writes things, answers things, or watches for things), tell me why, and let me agree or pick a different one.

Then run the hire skill for real, in team mode, and actually write the files, do not just describe what it would write. Ask its questions in the same one-thing-at-a-time way, and when I say "you pick" or "I don't know," take the recommended option and tell me which one you took.

When the hire is done, tell me the new employee's name, what it owns, and the exact first task I should hand it today.

To check it worked: ask the new employee (by name) to do that first real task, and see whether the result is usable without you rewriting it.

title: Follow-ups from a chat dump
does: Paste a week of client chats, get who is waiting on you, what you promised, and a draft reply for each.
prompt:
I want to know who is waiting on me.

Ask me one thing first: paste in the last few days of my client chats (copy from Messenger, WhatsApp, Viber, or email, one conversation after another, names included), or point you to a text file that has them.

Once you have the chats, go through every conversation and write a file called "followups-[today's date].md" with:
1. Every person who asked me something I have not answered yet, with the question in one line and how many days it has been waiting.
2. Every promise I made in those chats (a price, a file, a call, a date) that I have not delivered yet, one line each.
3. For each item in 1 and 2, a short draft reply in my tone, ready to paste back into the chat. Use the words I actually use in the chats, not a formal template.
4. At the top, the three replies to send first, and why those three.

Do not invent anything I did not say in the chats. If you are not sure whether something was answered, put it in a "not sure" list at the bottom instead of guessing.

When it is done, print the top three in the chat and tell me the file path.

To check it worked: open one of the chats it flagged and confirm the question really is still unanswered. If it flagged something you already replied to, tell Claude which one, so it learns what "answered" looks like in your chats.

Wrote followups-2026-09-16.md: three send-first items (overdue quote, address for delivery, oldest unanswered question), promises list, drafts in the chat's own tone, placeholders where a price or address was not in the chats instead of an invented one. title: SOP from a voice ramble
does: Paste a messy explanation of how you do a task, get a numbered SOP a new hire can follow without asking you.
prompt:
I want to turn the way I do one task into a written SOP my staff can follow.

Ask me one thing first: explain the task to me the way you would explain it out loud to a new hire, in one messy paragraph or a voice memo transcript, with every "and then" and "oh wait, before that" left in. Do not clean it up, I will do that.

Once I paste it, write a file called "sop-[short task name].md" with:
1. A one-line purpose: what this task is for and when it is done.
2. What you need before starting (accounts, files, tools, which passwords to ask for, never the passwords themselves).
3. The steps, numbered, one action per step, in the order they actually happen, not the order I said them in.
4. The places I said "usually" or "depends": turn each into an if-this-then-that line so the new hire does not have to ask.
5. A "done when" line: how the person knows the task is finished and who to tell.

Keep every step short enough to read while doing it. If I skipped something obvious (like logging in), add it and mark it with (added), so I can check it.

When it is done, print the numbered steps in the chat and tell me the file path.

To check it worked: hand the SOP to someone who has never done the task and watch them do it. Every place they stop to ask you a question is a step Claude should rewrite, tell it which one.
run_note: Ran clean (exit 0) on a one-paragraph payroll ramble. Wrote sop-payroll.md: purpose, before-you-start list, 12 numbered steps in the order they happen (login step marked added), overtime and cash-advance turned into if-then lines, GCash-down fallback, done-when line. title: App brief in 10 questions
does: Asks 10 questions and writes BRIEF.md: one screen that earns, who taps it, what it stores.
prompt:
I want to build a small app this weekend at Robots and Coffee, and I need a brief before any code gets written.

Ask me these 10 questions, one at a time, waiting for my answer before the next one:
1. In one sentence, what problem does this app solve.
2. Who is the one person that opens it (not "everyone," one real person).
3. What is the one screen that has to work for this to be worth building at all.
4. What does that person tap or type on that screen.
5. What does the app need to remember between visits.
6. Does it need to work with no internet at all, or is spotty internet fine.
7. Is there any money, PIN, or private info involved.
8. What does "it worked" look like at demo time, in one sentence.
9. What is explicitly out of scope for this weekend.
10. What is the name of the app, even a working name is fine.

After question 10, write a file called "BRIEF.md" that answers, in plain English:
- One screen that earns (the single screen that makes this worth building).
- Who taps it.
- What it stores.
- What is out of scope.
- The one-sentence demo-day success line.

Show me the finished BRIEF.md and ask if anything needs to change before we start building.

To check it worked: read BRIEF.md out loud in under 30 seconds. If you cannot explain your own app that fast, the brief is still too vague, tell Claude which line to sharpen.
run_note: Ran clean (exit 0) on the 10 sample answers passed as a pre-written file instead of an interview. Wrote BRIEF.md with the one-screen-that-earns, who taps it, what it stores, out of scope and the demo-day line, matching the DepositTrack sample answers.

title: PWA scaffold
does: One index.html plus manifest.webmanifest and sw.js, installable, offline shell, from BRIEF.md.
prompt:
Read BRIEF.md in this folder (if it does not exist yet, stop and tell me to run the app brief prompt first).

Build a PWA (a web app that can be installed on a phone like a real app) scaffold from that brief:
1. "index.html": one page, plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in that same file, no build tools, no npm install needed. It should show the one screen named in BRIEF.md and actually work when I double-click the file and open it in a browser.
2. "manifest.webmanifest": the app name, short name, start_url, display set to standalone, a background and theme color that make sense for the app, and icon entries at 192x192 and 512x512 (use plain colored placeholder icons if I have not given you real ones, and tell me that is what you did).
3. "sw.js": a small service worker that caches the app shell so it opens even with no internet, and always goes to the network for anything that looks like live data. Keep it short and comment why each part exists, do not add anything BRIEF.md did not ask for.
4. Link the manifest and register the service worker from index.html.

When it is done, tell me exactly how to open it locally to test (which command or which file to double-click), and what "it is installable" will look like once it is live on a real URL (the Add to Home Screen prompt will not appear on a plain local file, only after it is deployed with a valid manifest and service worker).

To check it worked: open index.html in your browser, open the browser's developer tools, and confirm no red errors show in the console.
run_note: Ran clean (exit 0) against a seeded BRIEF.md (DepositTrack). Wrote index.html, manifest.webmanifest, sw.js, plus icon-192.png and icon-512.png placeholders. Files present and non-empty after the run.

title: Data layer, localStorage first
does: Adds save and load with a versioned schema in localStorage and an export-to-JSON button; notes when to move to Supabase.
prompt:
Read BRIEF.md and index.html in this folder.

Add a data layer to the app using localStorage (data saved in the phone's browser, no server needed for this weekend).

Do this:
1. Design a simple schema for what BRIEF.md says the app needs to remember, and give it a version number, like { "version": 1, "items": [...] }.
2. Write save and load functions that read and write that schema to localStorage under one clearly named key.
3. Wire the app's screen to actually use save and load, so data survives closing and reopening the browser tab.
4. Add one button on the screen labeled "Export data" that downloads the current data as a .json file, so nothing is ever trapped only on one phone.
5. At the top of the script, write a short comment explaining the version number: when the schema changes later, bump the version and write a small function that upgrades old saved data to the new shape instead of losing it.

Do not add a database or any server code. If this app will ever need more than one person's data in one place (like a shared list, or login), say so in one paragraph and name Supabase as the next step, but do not build it now.

To check it worked: open the app, add some data, close the browser tab completely, reopen it, and confirm the data is still there. Then click Export data and confirm a .json file downloads with that same data in it.

title: PIN gate
does: A 4-digit PIN screen with SHA-256 via crypto.subtle, the honest limits of a client-side gate stated.
prompt:
Read BRIEF.md and index.html in this folder.

Add a simple PIN screen in front of the app.

Ask me one thing first: what 4-digit PIN should it use (or tell me to pick one and you will tell me what it is).

Then build:
1. A lock screen shown before the main app: a 4-digit PIN pad or input.
2. Hash the PIN with SHA-256 using the browser's built-in crypto.subtle (no library needed) and store only the hash in localStorage, never the plain PIN.
3. On entry, hash what was typed and compare it to the stored hash before showing the app.
4. After 5 wrong tries in a row, add a 30 second lock with a plain message, no scary language.

Before you finish, write me one short paragraph, in plain English, on what this PIN gate does and does not protect against: it stops someone glancing at the phone from opening the app, it does not stop someone who can open the browser's developer tools and read the page's own code, because there is no server here to hide anything behind. If this app will ever hold real money or private records for other people, that needs a real login on a real server, not this.

To check it worked: close the app, reopen it, confirm it asks for the PIN, confirm the wrong PIN is rejected, and confirm the right PIN opens the app.
run_note: not yet run, scheduled Sept 22 to 26

title: Deploy to GitHub Pages
does: git init, repo, Pages on main, the live URL, cache-busting check.
prompt:
I want this app folder live on the internet on a free URL by the end of this.

Ask me one thing first: what should the GitHub repository be called (lowercase, hyphens, no spaces).

Then do this yourself, do not just give me a list of commands to run:
1. Run git init in this folder if it is not already a git repo.
2. Create a .gitignore for anything that should not be committed (node_modules if present, .DS_Store, any local secret files).
3. Commit everything with a plain message.
4. Create the GitHub repository using the gh command (ask me to run "gh auth login" first if it is not already signed in, then continue once I confirm it is).
5. Push to the main branch.
6. Turn on GitHub Pages for this repo, serving from the main branch.
7. Wait for it to go live and tell me the exact live URL.

Once it is live, open the URL and confirm the page actually loads and looks like the app, not a blank page or a 404. If I make a change later and it does not show up on the live URL, that is a caching problem: tell me to do a hard refresh (shift-reload) before assuming anything is broken.

To check it worked: open the live URL on your phone's browser, not just your computer, and confirm the app loads there too.

title: Add-to-home-screen screen
does: An install screen with iPhone Safari and Android Chrome steps, shown only when not installed.
prompt:
Read index.html, manifest.webmanifest and sw.js in this folder.

Add a small "install this app" screen or banner that only shows when the app is not already installed (check for that with the standard display-mode: standalone media query, and hide the banner if it matches).

The banner should show two sets of plain steps, picked automatically based on the phone's browser if you can detect it, otherwise show both:
- iPhone Safari: tap the Share icon, then "Add to Home Screen," then "Add."
- Android Chrome: tap the three-dot menu, then "Add to Home screen" or "Install app," then confirm.

Keep the wording short, no jargon, and use the app's actual name from manifest.webmanifest so it is not generic. Add a small "not now" dismiss that does not show the banner again for that visitor (store that choice in localStorage).

To check it worked: open the live app on a phone, confirm the banner shows and the steps match the phone's browser, tap not now, reload the page, and confirm the banner stays hidden.

title: Reviewer QA loop
does: Spawns a reviewer agent from AgentKit against the app, fix-until-green, max 3 rounds.
prompt:
Read every file in this app folder.

Act as a strict code reviewer against this checklist: correctness (logic errors, broken buttons, anything that does not do what BRIEF.md promises), security (any secret or key committed into the code, any obvious way to break the PIN gate or the data layer), and basic quality (dead code, a file so long it is hard to follow, anything copy-pasted three times that should be one function).

Run this as a loop, up to 3 rounds:
1. Round 1: list every finding with a severity (critical, warning, info) and a one-line fix for each.
2. Fix every critical and warning finding yourself, directly in the files.
3. Round 2: review again from scratch, as if you had not seen round 1. List what is left.
4. Repeat once more if anything critical remains after round 2.
5. Stop after round 3 even if something remains, and tell me plainly what is still open and why it is safe to ship anyway or not.

At the end, print a short scorecard: how many findings in round 1, how many left at the end, and the ones you chose not to fix and why.

To check it worked: read the final scorecard and open the one or two files it flagged as most changed, and confirm the fix actually matches what was promised.
run_note: not yet run, scheduled Sept 22 to 26

title: Bug fix loop
does: Paste the bug, reproduce, root cause, one fix, one check.
prompt:
I found a bug. Here is what happened: [paste exactly what you did and what went wrong, as specific as you can be].

Do this in order, and show me each step, do not jump straight to a fix:
1. Reproduce it: read the relevant code and tell me the exact line or function where this breaks, and why, in plain English.
2. Root cause, not symptom: if this bug could happen from more than one place in the code, say so, and find the one shared place that actually causes it rather than patching just the spot I noticed.
3. One fix: make the smallest change that fixes the root cause. Do not refactor anything else while you are in there.
4. One check: after the fix, tell me exactly how to reproduce the original bug again to prove it is gone (the same steps I gave you in step 1), and run it yourself if you can.

When you are done, tell me in one line what was actually wrong (not just what I saw), and whether the same mistake could be hiding anywhere else in the app.

To check it worked: follow the exact reproduction steps from step 4 yourself and confirm the bug no longer happens.
run_note: not yet run, scheduled Sept 22 to 26

title: Demo day 2-minute script
does: Writes the 2-minute demo script from BRIEF.md: problem, tap, result, what is next.
prompt:
Read BRIEF.md in this folder.

Write a file called "DEMO-SCRIPT.md" that is a 2-minute spoken script for demo day, in my own plain voice, not a pitch-deck voice. Structure it in exactly four parts, timed so the whole thing runs about 2 minutes read out loud:
1. The problem (about 20 seconds): the real situation that made me build this, in one or two sentences.
2. The tap (about 60 seconds): walk through the actual screen live, in the order a real person would use it, saying out loud what I am tapping and why.
3. The result (about 20 seconds): what changed because of that one tap, stated plainly.
4. What is next (about 20 seconds): the one thing I would build next if I kept going, so it does not sound finished when it is a weekend build.

Write it as something I can read almost word for word without sounding robotic: short sentences, no jargon, no words I would not actually say out loud.

At the bottom, add a one-line backup plan for if the live demo breaks: what I say, and what I show instead (a screenshot or a recording, if I have one).

To check it worked: read the script out loud with a timer and confirm it lands close to 2 minutes without rushing.
